# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Introduction
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Objective
The objective of this analysis is to identify and examine factors associated with monthly rental prices in Tokyo's 23 wards using statistical methods.

This analysis explores a wide range of property characteristics, including location, floor area, building age, accessibility, layout, building structure, and housing facilities.

Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, hypothesis testing, and multiple regression analysis are used to investigate the relationships between these characteristics and rental prices.

The emphasis is on understanding and interpreting statistical relationships rather than maximizing predictive accuracy.



# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Libraries
# ------------------------------------------------------------
```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(car)
```



# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Data Overview
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.1 Load Data
```{r load-data}
# Load the preprocessed training dataset
df <- read.csv(
  "processed_train_data.csv",
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM"
)
```


# 3.2 Dataset Structure
```{r dataset-structure}
# Check dataset dimensions
cat("Number of observations:", nrow(df), "\n")
cat("Number of variables:", ncol(df), "\n")

# Examine variable names and data types
glimpse(df)
```



# 3.3 Missing Values
```{r missing-values}
# Calculate missing values for each variable
missing_summary <- df %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      list(
        missing_count = ~ sum(is.na(.x)),
        missing_rate = ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
    names_pattern = "^(.*)_(missing_count|missing_rate)$"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing_rate))


# Display missing values for all variables
missing_summary %>%
  mutate(missing_rate = round(missing_rate, 2)) %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c("Variable", "Missing Count", "Missing Rate (%)"),
    caption = "Missing Values by Variable"
  )
```



# 3.4 Descriptive Statistics
```{r descriptive-statistics} 
# Select key numerical variables with low missing rates
numeric_vars <- c(
  "rent",
  "area",
  "building_age",
  "floor",
  "total_floor",
  "walk_1"
)


# Summarize selected variables
summary(df[numeric_vars])
```

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Relationships Between Rent and Numerical Variables
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.1 Scatter Plots
```{r numerical-scatter-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
# Select numerical variables for exploratory analysis
plot_vars <- c("area", "building_age", "walk_1")


# Reshape data for visualization
scatter_data <- df %>%
  select(rent, all_of(plot_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(plot_vars),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )


# Plot relationships with monthly rent
ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = value, y = rent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationships Between Rent and Numerical Variables",
    x = "Property Characteristic",
    y = "Monthly Rent (JPY)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```



# 4.2 Correlation Analysis
```{r correlation-analysis}
# Select variables for correlation analysis
cor_vars <- c(
  "area",
  "building_age",
  "walk_1",
  "floor",
  "total_floor"
)


# Calculate Pearson and Spearman correlations with rent
correlation_results <- map_dfr(cor_vars, function(var) {

  complete_data <- df %>%
    select(rent, all_of(var)) %>%
    drop_na()

  tibble(
    variable = var,
    n = nrow(complete_data),
    pearson = cor(
      complete_data$rent,
      complete_data[[var]],
      method = "pearson"
    ),
    spearman = cor(
      complete_data$rent,
      complete_data[[var]],
      method = "spearman"
    )
  )
})


# Display correlation coefficients
correlation_results %>%
  mutate(across(c(pearson, spearman), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Pearson and Spearman Correlations with Monthly Rent"
  )
```



# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Relationships Between Rent and Categorical Variables
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.1 Rental Prices by Ward
```{r ward-summary}

  group_by(ward) %>%
  summarise(

    median_rent = median(rent, na.rm = TRUE),

# Display summary statistics
ward_summary %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(mean_rent, median_rent, sd_rent),
      ~ round(.x, 0)

  ) %>%

    caption = "Descriptive Statistics of Monthly Rent by Ward"

```

# 5.3 One-way ANOVA: Rent by ward
```{r one_way_anova_rent_by_ward}
# One-way ANOVA: Rent by ward
ward_anova <- aov(rent ~ ward, data = df)

summary(ward_anova)


# Eta-squared effect size
anova_table <- anova(ward_anova)

anova_table["ward", "Sum Sq"] / sum(anova_table[, "Sum Sq"])
```

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Multiple Regression Analysis
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.1 Model Specification
Multiple linear regression was used to examine the relationships between rental prices and property characteristics.

Log-transformed rent was used as the dependent variable. Three models were compared:

Model 1: Floor area, building age, and walking distance.

Model 2: Model 1 + ward.

Model 3: Model 2 + layout and building structure.


# 6.2 Baseline Regression
```{r model_1}
model_1 <- lm(
  log(rent) ~ area + building_age + walk_1,
  data = df
)

summary(model_1)
```


# 6.3 Controlling for Location
```{r model_2}
model_2 <- lm(
  log(rent) ~ area + building_age + walk_1 + ward,
  data = df
)

summary(model_2)
```



# 6.4 Property Characteristics
```{r model_3}
model_3 <- lm(
log(rent) ~ area + building_age + walk_1 +
ward + layout + building_structure,
data = df
)


# Display key regression coefficients
variables <- c("area", "building_age", "walk_1")

kable(
  coef(summary(model_3))[variables, , drop = FALSE],
  digits = 5,
  format.args = list(scientific = TRUE),
  caption = "Model 3: Key Regression Coefficients"
)


# Display adjusted R-squared
summary(model_3)$adj.r.squared
```
Model 3 additionally includes ward, layout, and building structure. Only the key numerical coefficients are displayed for readability.


# 6.5 Model Comparison
```{r model_comparison}
# Compare model fit
model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "Model 3"),
  Adjusted_R2 = c(
    summary(model_1)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(model_2)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(model_3)$adj.r.squared
  ),
  AIC = c(
    AIC(model_1),
    AIC(model_2),
    AIC(model_3)
  )
)

kable(
  model_comparison,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Comparison of Multiple Regression Models"
)


# Compare regression coefficients
variables <- c("area", "building_age", "walk_1")

coefficient_comparison <- data.frame(
  Variable = variables,
  Model_1 = coef(model_1)[variables],
  Model_2 = coef(model_2)[variables],
  Model_3 = coef(model_3)[variables],
  row.names = NULL
)

kable(
  coefficient_comparison,
  digits = 5,
  caption = "Comparison of Regression Coefficients"
)


# Compare 95% confidence intervals for key coefficients
variables <- c("area", "building_age", "walk_1")

ci <- confint(model_3, level = 0.95)

kable(
  data.frame(
    Variable = variables,
    Lower_95 = ci[variables, 1],
    Upper_95 = ci[variables, 2],
    row.names = NULL
  ),
  digits = 5,
  caption = "95% Confidence Intervals for Model 3"
)
```


# 6.6 Regression Findings
Floor area was positively associated with rent, while building age and walking distance showed negative associations.

Adding location and property characteristics improved the adjusted R² from 0.7348 to 0.9010.

The walking distance coefficient decreased in magnitude after controlling for ward, suggesting that location partly explains the observed relationship.



# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Regression Diagnostics
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 7.1 Residuals vs. Fitted Values
```{r residual_vs_fitted_values}
# Extract fitted values and residuals
diagnostic_df <- data.frame(
  fitted = fitted(model_3),
  residual = residuals(model_3)
)


# Residuals vs. Fitted Values
ggplot(diagnostic_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "red"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values",
    x = "Fitted Log Rent",
    y = "Residuals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 7.1 Findings
Residuals show a systematic downward pattern at higher fitted values, suggesting that the linear model does not fully capture the relationship between property characteristics and rental prices.

This indicates that nonlinear relationships may need to be considered in future predictive models.


# 7.2 Normal Q-Q Plot
```{r q_q_plot}
# Normal Q-Q Plot
ggplot(diagnostic_df, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
### 7.2 Findings

The residuals deviate from the theoretical normal distribution, particularly in the tails.

This suggests that the normality assumption is not fully satisfied, especially for extreme observations.


# 7.3 Influential Observations
```{r observations}
# Calculate Cook's distance
cooks_d <- cooks.distance(model_3)


# Identify observations with large Cook's distance
threshold <- 4 / nobs(model_3)

influential_summary <- data.frame(
  Threshold = threshold,
  Number_Above_Threshold = sum(cooks_d > threshold, na.rm = TRUE),
  Maximum_Cooks_Distance = max(cooks_d, na.rm = TRUE)
)

kable(
  influential_summary,
  digits = 6,
  caption = "Cook's Distance Summary"
)


# Identify the 10 most influential observations
top_10 <- order(cooks_d, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]

# Extract corresponding observations used in Model 3
model_data <- model.frame(model_3)

influential_properties <- data.frame(
  Observation = as.integer(rownames(model_data)[top_10]),
  Cook_Distance = cooks_d[top_10],
  Rent = exp(model.response(model_data)[top_10]),
  Area = model_data$area[top_10],
  Building_Age = model_data$building_age[top_10],
  Walk_1 = model_data$walk_1[top_10],
  Fitted_Rent = exp(fitted(model_3)[top_10])
)

kable(
  influential_properties,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Top 10 Influential Observations"
)


# Refit Model 3 without observation 20927
model_3_sensitivity <- update(
  model_3,
  data = df[-20927, ]
)


# Compare key coefficients
variables <- c("area", "building_age", "walk_1")

sensitivity_comparison <- data.frame(
  Variable = variables,
  Original = coef(model_3)[variables],
  Without_20927 = coef(model_3_sensitivity)[variables],
  row.names = NULL
)

kable(
  sensitivity_comparison,
  digits = 5,
  caption = "Sensitivity Analysis: Excluding Observation 20927"
)
```
### 7.3 Findings
Observation 20927 has a particularly large Cook's distance and produces an extreme fitted rental price.

Excluding this observation changes the floor area coefficient from 0.01484 to 0.01582, while the coefficients for building age and walking distance remain relatively stable.

This suggests that the estimated relationship between floor area and rent is sensitive to this influential observation.


# 7.4 Multicollinearity
```{r multicollinearity}
# Calculate variance inflation factors
vif_results <- car::vif(model_3)

vif_results
```
### 7.4 Findings
The adjusted GVIF values are relatively low for all predictors, with floor area having the highest value (2.20).

These results do not indicate severe multicollinearity in Model 3.



# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Conclusion
# ------------------------------------------------------------
This analysis identified floor area, building age, walking distance, and location as important factors associated with rental prices in Tokyo's 23 wards.

The final regression model achieved an adjusted R² of 0.9010. However, residual diagnostics revealed nonlinear patterns, deviations from normality, and influential observations.

These findings suggest that more flexible models may improve predictive performance and will guide the analysis in `03_modeling.Rmd`.
